passage: Tuesday night. Seema ma'am called us in today and said our output should double because "we have AI now." My chest went tight, but I kept my voice level. I asked for ten minutes and showed her a live run: the tool wrote a summary in one minute, then made up a number that wasn't in the source. She saw it. I told her every draft needs a review slot, or errors reach clients, and that I can't paste customer files into it because they're confidential. She wrote "review time" and "no customer data" in her notebook. We agreed on a trial: a modest increase, with a weekly check on error counts. Not what she first wanted, but she nodded. I'm tired, though a bit proud. — Leela

qa.q: What went wrong in the live run that Leela showed?
qa.a: The tool wrote a summary in one minute, then made up a number that wasn't in the source.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when Seema ma'am asked for doubled output?
qa.a: Leela's chest went tight, so she felt stressed, but she kept her voice level.

qa.q: What could Leela do if the trial shows errors rising?
qa.a: Bring the weekly error counts to Seema ma'am, explain what happened and ask to adjust the target while keeping the review slot.

qa.q: How did Seema ma'am seem to see AI at the start, and what changed?
qa.a: She seemed to assume AI would double output on its own. After the demonstration she wrote down review time and no customer data, and agreed to a trial.

grounding: A boss expects doubled output because AI exists; Leela shows what it can and cannot do, protects review time and flags risks including confidential data.

passage:
I'm Farida. Last year, my boss, Chandrika, came back from a conference and told our content team that with AI we should now produce twice as many articles a week, same hours.

I said yes. For two months I did it, quietly, working till eleven. Then an article went out with a made-up statistic the tool had invented. A reader caught it. I felt sick.

That's when I realised my silence had been the real mistake.

I asked Chandrika for a meeting. I brought examples: what the tool did well, like first drafts and headlines; what it did badly, like facts and tone. I pointed out that I'd almost pasted a client's private sales numbers into it once. I asked for protected time to review every piece.

She was surprised. She'd thought it was easy for us. We settled on one and a half times the output, with review built in. It's still a lot. But it's honest now.

qa.q: What did the tool invent in the article that went out?
How did Farida feel when the reader caught the error?
qa.a: Farida felt sick with guilt and worry about the mistake.

qa.q: What did Farida bring to the meeting, and why did it help?
qa.a: Examples of what the tool did well and badly, the risk to confidential data, and a request for review time, which gave Chandrika an honest picture.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see the workload after the meeting?
qa.a: Chandrika is surprised, having assumed AI made the work easy, and agrees to a more realistic target with review built in.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone whose boss expects doubled output because of AI, choosing to show what the tool can and cannot do, protect review time and flag risks.

passage:
Senior reviewer's note, loans team, week 6

Since the branch head announced that AI tools mean each officer should process thirty applications a day instead of fifteen, Ramesh has been staying until ten. Today I found him re-reading the same page three times, eyes red.

I asked how it was going. He admitted he'd been pasting customer documents into a public AI website to summarise them faster. He knew it might be against policy but felt he had no choice.

I stayed and we went through it together. We listed what the approved internal tool did well (summaries, form checks) and where it failed (odd income documents, anything needing judgement). We noted the confidential data risk.

Tomorrow Ramesh and I will present this to the branch head, with a realistic number and daily review time. I have also asked IT to confirm which tools are approved, so no one else is pushed into the same risk.

Jyoti

qa.q: How many applications a day were officers now expected to process?
What was Ramesh feeling when he admitted using the public AI website?
qa.a: He felt pressured and anxious, knowing it might break policy but feeling he had no choice.

qa.q: How did Jyoti support Ramesh, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Jyoti listed with him what the approved tool could and couldn't do, flagged the data risk, and planned to present a realistic target to the branch head together.

qa.q: How might the branch head be affected by the presentation?
qa.a: The branch head may be surprised by the risks and limits and may need to set more honest expectations.

grounding: A reviewer's note shows a young officer under pressure to double output because of AI, and a colleague helping him show the tool's limits, protect review time and flag data risks.
